change: Reference run: fastText embeddings fine-tuned, attention pooling, balanced class weights, first 400 words
hypothesis: Attention can focus on the few topic words in a long article, and fastText gives useful starting vectors for a 21k-article corpus.
With only ~21k training articles, pretrained Swahili vectors should beat learning embeddings from scratch.

change: fastText embeddings frozen instead of fine-tuned
hypothesis: fastText covers only 71% of the vocabulary and was trained on web text; fine-tuning should adapt vectors to news topics.

change: Max pooling over LSTM states instead of attention
hypothesis: Ablation: checks whether attention earns its extra parameters over a simpler pooling that also picks out strong topic features.

change: No class weights in the loss
hypothesis: Classes are 13x imbalanced; weighting the loss should raise recall on small classes (afya, uchumi) and so macro-F1.
Starting point: how far pure word counts go without any cleaning.

change: Cleaning: split glued sentences, repair ligatures, drop punctuation and numbers
hypothesis: Glued sentences create fake words like 'huu.misafara'; fixing them should help.
Function words carry little topic signal, so removing them may reduce noise.
Bigrams such as 'ligi kuu' or 'benki kuu' capture short local order.

change: ComplementNB (designed for imbalanced text), unigrams + bigrams
hypothesis: Multinomial NB favours the majority class 'kitaifa'; ComplementNB corrects this.

change: Final: ComplementNB alpha=0.03, cleaned text, unigrams + bigrams
hypothesis: Selected configuration, evaluated once on test.

change: Cleaned text, word unigrams + bigrams, no class weights
hypothesis: A discriminative linear model should beat Naive Bayes on the same features.
Weighting errors by inverse class frequency should raise recall on 'afya' and 'uchumi'.
